items.stem: A retention curve that flattens after several periods indicates what about the product?

options.text: A stable core of retained users has formed
options.rationale: Correct: a flattening curve shows a durable base of users who keep returning.
If everyone churned, retention would fall to zero, not flatten above it.
A flattening curve is a normal, interpretable pattern, not an error.
The curve itself is a retention measurement.

items.explanation: Correct: a flattening curve shows a durable base of users who keep returning.

items.stem: In RFM segmentation, the three dimensions are recency, frequency, and which third?

options.rationale: Correct: RFM stands for recency, frequency and monetary value.
Marketing channel is not part of RFM.
Session length is an engagement metric, not the M in RFM.
Mobile usage is not part of RFM.

items.stem: Which TWO pitfalls distort cohort comparisons? (Select TWO)

options.text: Comparing cohorts observed for different lengths of time
options.rationale: Correct: unequal observation windows make cohorts non-comparable.

options.text: Ignoring that early cohorts had more time to churn or convert
options.rationale: Correct: older cohorts have had more time, biasing a naive comparison.

options.text: Grouping users by their signup period
options.rationale: Grouping by signup period is the correct basis for cohorts.

options.text: Plotting retention as a percentage of the cohort
options.rationale: Plotting retention as a cohort percentage is standard and correct.

items.explanation: Correct: unequal observation windows make cohorts non-comparable.; Correct: older cohorts have had more time, biasing a naive comparison.
